column1: ROS SLR 精简编码表 / Concise Study Coding
一篇文章一行。主缺陷代码只填一个；其他缺陷代码可用分号列出，但每个 Full/Partial 缺陷必须在 02_Defect_Evidence 中单独建立证据行。缺陷覆盖度与研究质量不得混用。

column2: Article Title / 文章标题
column22: Adjudication / Notes

column2: A systematic review on cybersecurity of robotic systems: vulnerabilities trends, threats, attacks, challenges, and proposed framework
column22: Broad robotic-system cybersecurity review rather than a ROS-specific study. ROS 1 access control, encryption, authentication, and DoS weaknesses are explicitly synthesized from prior studies. ROS 2 is mentioned mainly as a limitation of an earlier secure-communication approach and through general DDS discussion; no ROS 2-specific defect is directly analyzed. The proposed framework is conceptual and not implemented or experimentally evaluated.

column2: Cyber security of robots: A comprehensive survey
column22: Broad survey of robot cybersecurity rather than a ROS-only study. ROS 1 and ROS 2 are both explicitly reviewed, but the codebook-matched defects concern mainly ROS 1 plaintext communication, unrestricted publishing/access, missing node authentication, and publicly exposed ROS instances. ROS 2 is principally discussed through DDS-Security, security APIs, mitigation mechanisms, and performance overhead; no sufficiently specific ROS 2 defect category is established. The paper reports seven databases, search period, inclusion/exclusion criteria, PRISMA counts, dual screening, and third-author adjudication, but omits exact database-specific queries, the complete extraction form, formal quality-assessment criteria, and a replication package.

column2: Robotics Cyber Security: Vulnerabilities, Attacks, Countermeasures, and Recommendations
column22: Broad narrative review of robotic cybersecurity rather than a ROS-specific or systematic review. ROS-specific discussion summarizes cryptographic protection for ROS communication and permission control over publishing, subscribing, and data consumption. No original ROS experiment, implementation, dataset, search protocol, quality assessment, or replication package is provided.

column2: An Empirical Study of Vulnerabilities in Robotics
column22: Empirical analysis of 176 CVE-confirmed robotics vulnerabilities from RVD. ROS is mentioned only as an example within the “Operating System Software” component type, which accounts for 4.8% of software-related vulnerabilities. The paper does not identify which records are ROS-related, distinguish ROS 1 from ROS 2, or cross-tabulate ROS records with the nine vulnerability categories. Therefore, no codebook leaf can be assigned without unsupported inference.

column2: Security in Robot Operating Systems (ROS): Analytical Review Study
column22: ROS security is the direct research object. The review compares ROS 1 and ROS 2 and synthesizes 32 studies, but provides no reproducible database-search procedure, selection criteria, extraction protocol, formal quality assessment, or replication package. ROS 1 access control, plaintext communication, anonymous node interaction, public exposure, and high-frequency publishing attacks are explicitly discussed. ROS 2 vulnerabilities are described only at a broad attack-category level and cannot be mapped reliably to the codebook’s mechanism-specific ROS 2 leaf codes.

column2: Who Controls Your Robot? An Evaluation of ROS Security Mechanisms
column22: The paper directly evaluates network-security properties of ROS 1, ROS 2, and ten protection mechanisms. It defines MITM and compromised-node attackers and evaluates confidentiality, metadata confidentiality, integrity/authenticity, access control, compatibility, and key exchange. No original protection tool or complete runtime attack experiment is presented. ROS2-ILE is primary because the plaintext transmission of SROS 2/DDS-Security policies and ROS metadata is the most specific mechanism-level deficiency established by the study.

column2: Robot Operating System 2: The Need for a Holistic Security Approach to Robotic Architectures
column22: The paper performs an architectural vulnerability analysis of ROS 2 and DDS-Security and experimentally evaluates security–performance trade-offs. The ROS translation layer is excluded from the benchmark; experiments measure RTI DDS messaging on one and two physical computers rather than a simulated robot. ROS2-ILE is primary because the paper directly demonstrates that security protection is independently configurable for discovery, liveliness, RTPS metadata, and payload, leaving selected information signed-only or completely unprotected. Credential/policy management, process isolation, and trusted security-component supply chains are identified as additional risks but are not experimentally exploited.

column2: Understanding Misconfigurations in ROS: An Empirical Study and Current Approaches
column22: ROS misconfigurations are the direct research object. The study analyzes 228 real ROS Answers questions, derives 12 high-level and 50 fine-grained categories, and maps them to 18 existing techniques. ICF is primary because the dominant fault families concern names, message contracts, missing endpoints, remapping, namespaces, launch wiring, parameters, and component composition. BSE covers incorrect physical or behavioral meanings, while SEF covers queues, frequency, stale data, synchronization, and launch race conditions. Only 37 of 228 questions identify a ROS version, making version-specific classification infeasible; therefore, Unclear is more defensible than Both. The dataset is publicly released, but the tool-review evaluation is limited to selected venues and 2018–2022, and only 10 of 18 technique mappings received external author validation.

column2: The Role of Security in Human-Robot Shared Environments: A Case Study in ROS-based Surveillance Robots
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-UTA; ROS1-SPF; ROS1-LFQ
column22: The paper directly analyzes ROS 1 security weaknesses and uses the STOP multi-robot surveillance architecture as a case study. The primary weakness is unrestricted access to topics, nodes, and robot commands. Plaintext communication, missing node authentication, absent QoS/flow control, and the centralized ROS Master bottleneck are also explicitly discussed. The proposed hierarchical protections are largely design recommendations and ongoing implementation plans; the paper does not experimentally attack the STOP system or evaluate the proposed mechanisms quantitatively.

column2: A Study on ROS Vulnerabilities and Countermeasure
column22: The study experimentally analyzes ROS Indigo. An attacker joins the target ROS graph by configuring ROS_MASTER_URI, remotely controls TurtleSim, records and replays KOBUKI control messages, observes unencrypted communication, and replaces an existing service through duplicate-name registration. The attacks do not require application source code, although ROS Master source code is inspected to explain the service-hijacking mechanism.

column2: Smart Malware that Uses Leaked Control Data of Robotic Applications: The Case of Raven-II Surgical Robots
column22: The attack targets ROS 1 Kinetic and uses a malicious external ROS node to subscribe to sensitive state topics, infer critical surgical stages with DBSCAN, terminate or replace a legitimate publisher through a duplicate node name, and inject corrupted sensor/control data. The evaluation covers three simulated surgical scenarios, quantitative trigger accuracy, three fault payloads, and a safety module. Target application source code is not required, but the attacker needs network access, ROS APIs, relevant topic names, message structures, and some application knowledge.

column2: ROSploit: Cybersecurity Tool for ROS
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-UTA; ROS1-SPF; ROS1-LFQ
column22: The paper presents a modular offensive tool with reconnaissance and exploitation components. ROSploit scans the ROS Master and arbitrary ports, enumerates nodes, topics, and services, and supports topic-level MITM attacks that can modify communications. The target application source code is not required. Evaluation is limited to a qualitative comparison between ROSploit scan results and the native ROS graph; no quantitative exploit evaluation, test repetitions, complete experimental configuration, or public replication package is reported.

column2: Scanning the Internet for ROS: A View of Security in Robotics Research
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-UTA; ROS1-IPS; ROS1-SPF
column22: The study performs three Internet-wide scans for ROS Masters on TCP port 11311 and one scan for Rosbridge on port 9090. Each Master scan identified more than 100 publicly accessible ROS instances across 28 countries. With owner consent, the authors accessed camera and point-cloud data, published actuator commands, moved a robot neck, and modified ROS parameters. Application source code was not required for scanning or standard topic access, although a custom .srv definition was needed to call one robot-specific service. Publicly visible simulators were measured, but the authors’ proof-of-concept evaluation used physical robots rather than a simulation testbed.

column2: Security on ROS: Analyzing and Exploiting Vulnerabilities of ROS-Based Systems
column22: The study implements and evaluates a network MITM tool against the physical DoRIS domestic robot. Through ARP poisoning, IP forwarding, Netfilter Queue and Scapy, the attacker intercepts, reads, modifies or drops ROS topic packets exchanged between the robot and an external processing server. ROS1-LE is primary because the demonstrated attack fundamentally relies on ROS 1 transmitting data without encryption or cryptographic integrity protection. The paper also explicitly identifies missing node authentication and topic authorization, but those mechanisms are not independently exploited through ROS Master registration in the reported experiment.

column2: Security Controller Synthesis for ROS-based Robot
column22: The paper synthesizes task and security controllers from TLSF/LTL specifications using a GR(1)-based algorithm. It addresses false-command injection enabled by unrestricted ROS topic publishing and DoS attacks characterized by abnormal message volume and resource consumption. The Gazebo evaluation demonstrates controller responses and task continuation using standby robots, but does not report a concrete ROS attack implementation, traffic-generation parameters, detection accuracy, false-positive rate, repeated trials, or physical-robot evaluation.

column2: Penetration Testing ROS
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-UTA; ROS1-IPS; ROS1-SPF; ROS1-LFQ
column22: The chapter presents ROSPenTo and Roschaos for attacking ROS 1 Master, Slave, Parameter Server, topic, service, action and node-management APIs. It experimentally demonstrates stealth publisher injection, publisher/subscriber isolation, service isolation, malicious parameter updates and remote node shutdown. Examples include ROS Kinetic tutorial systems, a physical KUKA iiwa safety application with an OMRON OS32c LIDAR, and a Gazebo TurtleBot navigation simulation. No target application source code is required for graph analysis and API manipulation, although valid data injection requires the ROS message definition and parameter attacks require knowledge of parameter subscriptions.

column2: Novel Denial-of-Service Attacks Against Cloud-Based Multi-Robot Systems
column22: The study implements three DoS attacks against ROS Melodic cloud-based multi-robot workloads: network flooding, micro-architecture contention, and parameter manipulation. ROS1-LFQ is the only precise codebook match because a malicious publisher can increase its rate from 4 Hz to 400 Hz, fill router queues, increase latency and packet loss, and force subscribers to consume excessive resources. Hardware evaluations use two robot-computing platforms and a virtualized cloud server; two end-to-end case studies use Gazebo and RViz. The target application source code is not required, although the attacker must control or compromise one function node and understand relevant topics or performance parameters.

column2: Data Tampering Attack Design for ROS-Based Object Detection and Tracking Robotic Platform
column22: The paper experimentally attacks a physical ROS 1 mobile robot. A TCPROS MITM attack intercepts the plaintext 48-byte /cmd_vel payload and modifies linear and angular velocity values, changing the robot trajectory. A second Python tool exploits unauthenticated Master/Slave XML-RPC APIs, retrieves the ROS graph, forges publisherUpdate, and connects a fake image publisher to the object-detection node. The target application source code is not required, although the attacker needs the topic, message type, payload structure, ROS Master address, and ROS API knowledge. The paper reports “ROS Kinect distribution,” which appears to refer to ROS Kinetic; the generation is unambiguously ROS 1.

column2: Analysis of Attacks on Robotic Operation System
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-UTA; ROS1-IPS; ROS1-SPF; ROS1-LFQ
column22: The study experimentally exploits missing authentication in the ROS 1 Master and Slave XML-RPC APIs using ROS Kinetic, Docker, roschaos and ROSPenTo. It demonstrates unauthorized publisher deregistration and manipulation of subscriber publisher lists. It also explicitly discusses plaintext ROS 1 communication and residual ROS 2/DDS-Security leakage, but does not experimentally validate the encryption-related weaknesses. The evaluation is limited to small synthetic ROS publisher/subscriber scenarios and reports no quantitative metrics or physical robot validation.

column2: Cyberattacks on Self-Driving Cars and Surgical and Eldercare Robots
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-UTA; ROS1-SPF; ROS1-LFQ
column22: The paper directly reviews ROS security weaknesses and ROS-based attacks in surgical and eldercare robots. Unauthorized publishing and arbitrary topic access are selected as the primary defect family. Missing authentication, plaintext communication and malicious high-rate publishing are separate vulnerability families. ROS real-time latency, message loss and lack of scheduling guarantees constitute a distinct reliability concern. The paper is a narrative review without a reported search strategy, screening process, quality assessment, original experiment or replication package.

column2: ROS Network Security for a Swing Doors Automation in a Robotized Hospital
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-UTA; ROS1-SPF; ROS1-LFQ
column22: The paper directly analyzes ROS 1 message-transfer security in a robotized hospital. TCPROS plaintext transmission and healthcare-data confidentiality are the primary concerns. Authentication and authorization are explicitly identified as additional requirements. The authors compare centralized, mixed and independent architectures and recommend a fully centralized, isolated network with WPA2/WPA3, authentication, authorization, encryption, firewall protection and backup servers. However, no implemented prototype, attack experiment, performance measurement or replication artifact is reported.

column2: An Analysis of DoS Attack on Robot Operating System
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-UTA; ROS1-SPF; ROS1-LFQ
column22: The paper directly evaluates ROS 1 DoS attacks using ROS Noetic, Gazebo, TurtleBot3 Waffle, ROSPloit, custom publisher/subscriber attacks and Tshark. Attack volumes of 10, 100 and 1000 malicious nodes are evaluated under four background-traffic levels. Delay and packet loss are measured at the application and transport layers. No target source code is required. Evaluation is simulation-only. Reproducibility is limited because the custom attack implementation, scripts and collected traffic dataset are not publicly provided.

column2: Understanding the Internet-Wide Vulnerability Landscape for ROS-based Robotic Vehicles
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-UTA; ROS1-IPS; ROS1-SPF; ROS2-ILE; ROS2-LMLAC; ROS2-ICAPP; ROS2-MPIB; ROS2-UTFAN
column22: The study directly measures Internet-exposed ROS 1 systems through three IPv4-wide scans and deploys 38 ROS 1/ROS 2 honeypots. Public exposure is the primary defect. Missing authentication and unrestricted ROS access are explicit enabling weaknesses, but the authors deliberately avoid modifying scanned systems or retrieving sensitive payload data. Code and data are publicly released.

column2: Analyzing Impact and Systemwide Effects of the SlowROS Attack in an Industrial Automation Scenario
column12: ROS1-LE; ROS1-PNE; ROS1-LNA; ROS1-IPS; ROS1-SPF; ROS1-LFQ
column22: The study directly discovers and evaluates a Slow DoS vulnerability in the standard ROS Noetic Master. The primary root cause is the absence of an effective idle-connection timeout, enabling malicious connections to occupy all available sockets and file descriptors indefinitely. Because the ROS Master and Parameter Server share one process and the Master is centralized, resource exhaustion causes systemwide disruption. Evaluation uses a physical Interbotix PincherX-100 arm, Intel NUC, Raspberry Pi nodes and a 100BaseTX industrial network. Experimental procedures and parameters are detailed, but the attack software and raw data are not publicly released; data are available only on request.

column2: Network Reconnaissance and Vulnerability Excavation of Secure DDS Systems
column22: The direct object is Secure DDS rather than a complete ROS 2 deployment, but the analyzed DDS-Security mechanism is used by ROS 2 and the paper explicitly discusses ROS 2 topic naming and fingerprinting. Permission documents are exchanged in plaintext during the authenticated crypto handshake, exposing topic, partition, data-tag and capability metadata. The authors implement a reproducible Docker-based test harness, capture RTPS traffic, reconstruct DDS information-flow topology with formal verification, and release the code publicly.

column2: AVGuardian: Detecting and Mitigating Publish-Subscribe Overprivilege for Autonomous Vehicle Systems
column22: The paper directly studies coarse-grained publish/subscribe permissions in ROS-based autonomous-vehicle systems. SROS correctly enforces topic/message-level policies, but authorized modules receive unnecessary read or write authority over individual message fields. ROS1-UTA is the closest valid ROS 1 code, although the exact mechanism is message-field-level overprivilege. The concept resembles ROS2-LMLAC, but that code cannot be used because the implementation and evaluation use ROS Indigo. AVGuardian requires target module source code and evaluates attacks using Apollo SimControl and real-world driving traces. The paper provides video demonstrations but does not report a public release of the AVGuardian implementation or complete reproduction package.

column2: Analyzing Security Vulnerability and Forensic Investigation of ROS2: A Case Study
column22: The paper directly evaluates ROS 2 Foxy security using a victim VM and an attacker VM. A malicious ROS 2 client joins the same communication domain, invokes the victim service without prior authorization and sends repeated requests until the service crashes. ROS2-UTFAN is the closest existing leaf because the observed availability failure is caused by unrestricted service-client traffic. However, DDS-Security authentication is not enabled, so the paper does not strictly study traffic abuse by a cryptographically authenticated node. Unauthorized service access and data injection are also demonstrated, but the current ROS 2 codebook contains no direct equivalent of ROS1-UTA. The attack commands are described, but package names, the DoS script, request rate, repetition count and complete artifacts are not provided.

column2: Investigating Security Threats in Multi-Tenant ROS 2 Systems
column12: ROS2-ILE; ROS2-LMLAC; ROS2-ICAPP; ROS2-MPIB; ROS2-UTFAN; ROS2-LRI
column22: The paper directly investigates ROS 2 node, topic, namespace, Domain ID and SROS2 enclave security in multi-tenant environments. The primary weakness is the insufficient protection and binding of security contexts/enclaves: malicious nodes can create new contexts through internal APIs or CLI tools, override enclave settings and escape inherited restrictions. Topic-level permission granularity, missing publisher-source binding and the insecure ROS 1 side of ros1_bridge form additional independent weaknesses. Experiments use Open-RMF, Autoware and a ROS1–ROS2 camera application in software environments. The paper describes configurations and attacks clearly, but does not provide a complete public reproduction package or attack-tool repository.

column2: Cybersecurity in Autonomous Systems: Evaluating the Performance of Hardening ROS
column22: The study directly evaluates the confidentiality weakness of ROS 1 Indigo communications and implements separate encryption/decryption nodes using 3DES. A malicious ROS node can discover the ROS Master and subscribe to the sensor topic, but cannot recover the protected payload without the key. Evaluation includes publisher/listener tests, 256 KB–1 MB messages, and an 18-hour camera experiment with 971,790 frames. Source code and raw data are not released, limiting complete reproduction.

column2: Cybersecurity in Autonomous Systems: Hardening ROS Using Encrypted Communications and Semantic Rules
column22: The paper directly studies ROS 1 plaintext communication and implements AES encryption plus ROSRV runtime monitors. A second publisher can inject plaintext messages into the same topic, while the monitor detects and discards them. A separate monitor rejects localization messages affected by an external DoS attack against the KIO RTLS. Evaluation uses a physical robot and real localization hardware. Public source code is provided. Method clarity is reduced by an inconsistency between the prose and Algorithm 1 regarding the chi-square threshold, and the evaluation reports proof-of-concept outcomes rather than systematic detection accuracy.

column2: Increasing ROS 1.x Communication Security for Medical Surgery Robot
column22: The paper directly studies missing authentication and authorization in ROS 1.x. It implements an application-layer AA node, a database-connector node, runtime communication keys, login/logout services and authorization checks for publishing and subscribing. Adoption requires ROS nodes to use overloaded subscribe/advertise functions. Evaluation is a software prototype on Ubuntu 14.04 and ROS Indigo; no robot simulator or physical surgical procedure is used. Functional testing is described, but attack coverage, latency measurements, repeated trials, source-code release and raw data are not provided.

column2: Application-level Security for ROS-based Applications
column22: The paper directly addresses missing node and message authentication in ROS 1. A dedicated authentication server performs certificate-based challenge–response authentication, distributes topic-specific keys and provides publisher verification. Unauthorized publishing, arbitrary subscription and plaintext communication are separate weaknesses. Evaluation uses a physical KUKA iiwa and compares insecure and secured execution, but provides no repeated trials, attack-success statistics or released implementation package.

column2: Security for the Robot Operating System
column22: The paper systematically analyzes unauthorized publishing, arbitrary subscription, insecure XMLRPC calls, plaintext node communication, high-rate message flooding and parameter manipulation in ROS 1. It implements two defenses: an application-level authentication/encryption architecture and a ROS Kinetic roscpp modification using TLS/DTLS and certificate-based topic authorization. RosPenTo is used to reconstruct and manipulate the ROS graph and inject false information. Source access is required for the secure-channel modification, although RosPenTo itself is black-box. Attack and mitigation procedures are detailed, but the complete implementation, scripts and experimental datasets are not packaged as a fully self-contained replication artifact.

column2: Policy-based Access Control for Robotic Applications
column22: The paper directly studies the absence of permission control in ROS 1. It proposes and implements a PBAC access manager with identity tokens, access tokens, policy evaluation and runtime revocation. The method requires modifying or adapting ROS/application code so that resources verify access tokens. Evaluation uses a Pioneer 3-DX robot, three access-control scenarios and 1,000 performance requests. Evaluation is limited to one platform, simple cases and overhead measurements; no public repository, complete source code or detailed policy scripts are provided.

column2: Cross-Layer Secure and Resilient Control of Delay-Sensitive Networked Robot Operating Systems
column22: The paper directly models false-data injection against ROS agents and designs a lightweight MAC, time-delay controller, Chi-square detector and POMDP-based security policy. ROS is the stated application context, but the dynamics, authentication model and numerical evaluation are largely generic networked-control abstractions rather than a ROS protocol implementation. Evaluation is numerical only, without an executable ROS tool, ROS distribution, communication trace, physical robot or simulator.

column2: Designing a Security Platform for Collaborating Autonomous Systems – An Experience Report
column22: The paper designs and implements an application-layer security platform for collaborative TurtleBots using ROS 1. It addresses unauthenticated ROS Master–node interaction, unrestricted message/service access and unencrypted communication through OAuth-based authentication and authorization, TLS, public-key encryption, REST services and fault-tolerance mechanisms. The implementation architecture is clearly described, but evaluation is mainly an experience report and illustrated case study without attack-detection metrics, performance benchmarks, comparative baselines or a public replication package.

column2: Message Authentication Codes for Secure Remote Non-Native Client Connections to ROS Enabled Robots
column22: The paper directly addresses the lack of authentication for remote rosbridge clients. It implements the rosauth package, modifies the rosbridge protocol, uses SHA-512 MAC-based tokens and SSL/WSS, and validates authorized and unauthorized connection attempts on PR2 and KUKA youBot systems. Public Internet exposure and plaintext communication are directly discussed and mitigated. Fine-grained publish/subscribe authorization is explicitly identified but deferred to future work.

column2: A Cryptography-Powered Infrastructure to Ensure the Integrity of Robot Workflows
column22: The study protects generic robot workflows against intentional or unauthorized modification using Merkle trees, RSA signatures and an external compliance service. ROS is not the primary execution model: the authors explicitly exclude fully distributed ROS applications from the central workflow model, although ROS drivers, actions, services and publications can be encapsulated as workflow components. The evaluated CHIMERA stack may use either a ROS-based MiR driver or a REST driver, and no ROS distribution or version is specified. Consequently, none of the fixed ROS 1/ROS 2 vulnerability leaf codes precisely represents the studied root cause.

column2: AuthROS: Secure Data Sharing Among Robot Operating Systems Based on Ethereum
column22: The study implements an additional ROS node and an Ethereum-based data-sharing layer for ROS Melodic robots. SM4 encryption protects ROS data, SM2 signatures authenticate data sources and SM3/blockchain digests verify integrity. Smart contracts implement identity registration and authority granting. However, AuthROS does not modify native ROS Master registration or directly enforce access control on the original ROS topic graph. Security evaluation concentrates mainly on cryptographic and blockchain performance rather than systematic attack success rates.

column2: Proposed Technique for Data Security with the AES Algorithm in Robot Operating System (ROS)
column22: The paper directly analyzes plaintext TCPROS communication and implements the L2Topic application-layer encryption method using AES-256, OpenSSL, JSON and std_msgs::String. Plain and encrypted packets are inspected with Wireshark. Evaluation compares encrypted and unencrypted image streaming at four resolutions using frame rate, encryption/decryption time and CPU utilization. The evaluation is limited to one communication workload and does not report systematic attack tests, repeated statistical analysis, key-management security or comparisons with SROS/Secure ROS. No complete implementation repository is provided.

column2: Procedurally Provisioned Access Control for Robotic Systems
column22: The paper develops ComArmor and Keymint for defining, compiling and verifying ROS 2/DDS access-control policies. It experimentally demonstrates that ROS 2 Ardent namespace-to-DDS mapping and an SROS2 empty-partition workaround can generate unintended permissions and cross-talk between ROS 2 subsystems. It also identifies gratuitous permissions in the default SROS2 template. The implementation, policy language, verification procedure and experiment materials are publicly available.

column2: Enhancing Security in ROS
column22: The chapter directly addresses missing ROS 1 graph-level access control and proposes security logging, automatically generated policy profiles, X.509 identity/attribute certificates, and user-pull/server-pull certificate architectures. Authentication and encryption are substantial secondary concerns. The work is primarily architectural and conceptual: no implemented prototype, ROS testbed, attack experiment, performance result, public tool, or replication package is reported.

column2: Runtime Verification on Hierarchical Properties of ROS-Based Robot Swarms
column22: The implementation explicitly uses Ubuntu 16.04 and ROS Kinetic, therefore it is coded as ROS 1. RMoM monitors author-defined resource, communication, robot-behavior, and swarm-behavior properties. Behavioral and swarm-property violations are the main research object; unauthorized publishing by a bogus ROS node is an independently evaluated security case. The method consumes runtime ROS topics, node information, resource states, and user-written properties rather than target application source code. Evaluation includes a physical TurtleBot and a Gazebo UAV-swarm simulation. No public RMoM source-code repository is reported.

column2: CryptoROS: A Secure Communication Architecture for ROS-Based Applications
column22: The study explicitly targets ROS 1, as shown by its reliance on ROS Master, XML-RPC, TCPROS, rospy, and roscpp. CryptoROS proposes TLS-secured peer-to-peer communication and token-based authentication and authorization without modifying target ROS nodes or client libraries. However, the architecture is not implemented or experimentally evaluated; implementation and performance measurement are left to future work. XML-RPC traffic and the ROS Master remain unprotected.

column2: TROS: Protecting Humanoids’ ROS from Privileged Attackers
column22: TROS extends ROS Melodic C++ with Intel SGX enclaves to protect ROS messages, encryption keys, node identities, topic-subscription records, configuration data and ROS entity URIs against privileged local attackers. The system is evaluated through memory-dump and DMA attacks, performance experiments, and two misuse cases involving a V-REP simulated NAO. ROS 2 is directly analyzed regarding exposed certificates and permission data, but is not implemented or experimentally evaluated. No public TROS repository or complete replication package is reported.

column2: SROS2: Usable Cyber Security Tools for ROS 2
column22: SROS2 is an open-source ROS 2 security toolchain that generates and manages Identity CA, Permissions CA, X.509 certificates, governance files, permission files and enclave artifacts. It also supports graph introspection, automatic policy generation and DDS/RTPS security monitoring. The TurtleBot3 case study is conducted in simulation. The study identifies usability, secure distribution and credential-lifecycle limitations, but does not experimentally evaluate credential or policy tampering.

column2: ROSEC: Intra-Process Isolation for ROS Composition With Memory Protection Keys
column22: The study targets the absence of memory isolation among ROS 2 composable nodes sharing a container process. ROSEC modifies the ROS 2 client library and executor, and uses Intel MPK, per-node allocators, separate stacks and dynamic protection-key assignment to isolate heap, stack and global objects. Evaluation uses ROS 2 Dashing on physical x86 hardware, synthetic ROS 2 workloads and a real camera-based image_tools application. No public ROSEC source-code repository or complete replication package is reported.

column2: Support Remote Attestation for Decentralized Robot Operating System (ROS) Using Trusted Execution Environment
column22: The paper identifies the DDS Security assumption that local machines and locally stored credentials, keys, policies and configuration files are trustworthy. It proposes placing DDS and security artifacts inside SCONE/SGX enclaves and using remote attestation to continuously verify node identity and integrity. The design is conceptual: no ROS 2 prototype, attack experiment, performance evaluation or public implementation is reported.

column2: Quantifying DDS-Cerberus Network Control Overhead
column22: The implementation uses ROS 2 Foxy, DDS and Kerberos V5 on a laptop and two Raspberry Pi devices. DDS-C requires each publisher and subscriber to possess a node-specific Kerberos principal and keytab and authenticate before DDS operations. The evaluation rigorously measures authentication traffic overhead under different node counts, network arrangements and QoS reliability settings. However, it assumes that nodes authenticate successfully and that no node is compromised; therefore, impersonation resistance is not directly tested through an adversarial experiment.

column2: Decentralized Information-Flow Control for ROS2
column22: The paper directly targets the inability of ROS 2 and SROS2 topic-level permissions to control downstream use and re-publication of protected data. Picaros implements data-object-level decentralized information-flow control using DIFC labels and decentralized multi-authority attribute-based encryption. It modifies rclcpp, adds a loadable kernel module and verification service, and evaluates latency, memory and power overhead using ROS 2 Humble, SROS2 and iRobot application benchmarks. No public Picaros implementation or complete replication package is reported.

column2: ROSRV: Runtime Verification for Robots
column22: The implementation uses ROS Groovy on Ubuntu 12.04 and depends on the ROS Master, XML-RPC requests and ROS 1 topic communication. ROSRV generates runtime monitors from formal safety specifications and enforces host-level access-control policies for node creation, publishing, subscribing and ROS commands. It was demonstrated on a commercial LandShark UGV with legal and attacker nodes. The paper reports public source code, materials and demonstrations, but provides limited quantitative evaluation and no systematic baseline comparison.

column2: ROSMonitoring: A Runtime Verification Framework for ROS
column22: ROSMonitoring supports ROS Kinetic and Melodic and monitors ROS topic communication against user-defined formal properties. The Curiosity rover case study filters unsafe wheel commands according to speed and movement direction. A separate scalability experiment evaluates 10 nodes, 10 topics and message rates up to 10,000 messages/s. The framework modifies launch/remapping configuration but does not require target application source-code analysis or modification. Source code and examples are publicly available.

column2: ROS-Defender: SDN-Based Security Policy Enforcement for Robotic Applications
column22: The study targets ROS 1 and SROS1 architectures based on ROS Master, Parameter Server, XML-RPC, TCPROS/UDPROS and SROS. ROS-Defender maps ROS-level topic, node and service policies to OpenFlow flow rules and dynamically blocks unauthorized or anomalous connections. It is implemented with Ryu, OpenFlow 1.3, Open vSwitch/Zodiac WX and ROSWatch. Evaluation covers a physical TurtleBot3 and several Gazebo/Mininet robot simulations, but mainly measures performance overhead rather than attack-detection accuracy or security bypass resistance.

column2: Towards a Robotic Intrusion Prevention System: Combining Security and Safety in Cognitive Social Robots
column22: The study designs a ROS 2 robotic intrusion-prevention framework that monitors message events, graph changes, publisher/subscriber identities, topic structure and payloads, and then maps detected threat levels to safety-oriented System Modes. The physical evaluation uses a TIAGo robot with ROS 2 Foxy/Humble and CycloneDDS. However, the RIPS detection core is emulated: the experiments validate system reconfiguration after a simulated intrusion signal, rather than actual detection of malicious ROS 2 traffic. A fully functional ROS 2 monitor and rule engine are left to future work.

column2: Watch Your Callback: Offline Anomaly Detection Using Machine Learning in ROS 2
column22: The operational target is abnormal callback execution response time and invocation frequency, directly corresponding to ROS 2 execution and scheduling behavior. Four synthetic DoS scenarios are evaluated by altering callbackJointState; benign anomalies are approximated through augmentation of normal traces. The detection method uses built-in ros2_tracing tracepoints and does not require modification of monitored node source code, although reproducing the seeded attack scenarios requires modifying the selected callback. Evaluation is Gazebo-only and uses an internally generated, non-public dataset.

column2: Intrusion Detection on Robot Cameras Using Spatio-Temporal Autoencoders: A Self-Driving Car Application
column22: The paper models a malicious ROS node that publishes, intercepts, modifies, replays, or floods images on a camera topic. Ten author-created attack scenarios are evaluated using camera frames extracted from a public Udacity ROSBAG dataset. The detection model is image-based and can operate without the source code of ROS nodes. No ROS distribution is named; ROS 1 is inferred from the ROSBAG/Autoware-era architecture and the absence of DDS or ROS 2 mechanisms.

column2: Detecting Data Injection Attacks in ROS Systems Using Machine Learning
column22: The evaluated attack is unauthorized publishing of false motion commands to /cmd_vel. A fake node is added to the publisher list through publisherUpdate and publishes malicious commands at 10 Hz. The proposed NIDS uses Tcpdump/Tcpstat network statistics and an SVM classifier, so target application source code is not required. Evaluation is limited to one simulated SLAM scenario and one attack family.

column2: Trusted Operations of a Military Ground Robot in the Face of Man-in-the-Middle Cyberattacks Using Deep Learning Convolutional Neural Networks: Real-Time Experimental Outcomes
column22: The paper explicitly studies ROS 1.0 and performs a real-time attack on a physical GVR-BOT. Malicious ROS traffic overwrites legitimate /cmd_vel guidance data, causing loss of control. The IDS uses 33 runtime ROS/network and robot-state features transformed into RGB or grayscale images and classified by CNN. No target application source code is required. Experiments include indoor and outdoor physical operation, multiple robot motions, voting filters, two windowing schemes, and comparisons with BoF and SVM.

column2: DCWM-LSTM: A Novel Attack Detection Framework for Robotic Arms
column22: The evaluated system explicitly uses ROS-Master, attacker-created ROS nodes, ROS topics and rosbag data, therefore it is coded as ROS 1. The replay attack records data obtained through an unauthorized subscription and republishes it continuously to the target. The subscriber-flood attack repeatedly sends subscription requests, causing ROS-Master overload, delayed arm movement and temporary unresponsiveness. DCWM-LSTM operates on runtime joint-state data and does not require target application source code. Experiments use a physical Kawasaki RS05L arm in the IFARLab-DIH factory laboratory.

column2: ROZZ: Property-based Fuzzing for Robotic Programs in ROS
column22: ROZZ performs source-level LLVM instrumentation, distributed branch-coverage collection, multidimensional input mutation and temporal message mutation. The main evaluation covers 10 ROS 2 Foxy programs and finds 43 real implementation bugs; an additional ROS 1 evaluation finds six bugs. All reported bugs are implementation-level memory, exception-handling or synchronization defects. The experiments use Gazebo and a virtual TurtleBot3.

column2: Multi-Dimensional and Message-Guided Fuzzing for Robotic Programs in Robot Operating System
column22: ROFER tests 13 ROS 2 Foxy programs written in C++ and Python. It uses multidimensional mutation over user commands, configuration parameters, sensor-message data and message order, together with message-feature feedback. The study reports 88 real bugs, including null-pointer dereferences, use-after-free defects, buffer/stack overflows, invalid-pointer accesses and unhandled exceptions; 46 were confirmed by developers. ROFER itself can test closed-source programs without code instrumentation, although the evaluation uses llvm-cov and ASan for C++ coverage and memory-bug diagnosis.

column2: Toward the Trustworthiness of Industrial Robotics Using Differential Fuzz Testing
column22: The evaluation uses Ubuntu 16.04 and ROS Kinetic. RROSFuzz compares two MoveIt! interfaces implementing the same forward-kinematics and robot-arm movement function. Among 15,246 test cases, 9,266 produce inconsistent outputs. The authors conclude that moveit_commander.arm.go() can mishandle joint angles, preventing the arm from accurately reaching the requested pose. The general differential method executes package interfaces and compares outputs without requiring target source code, although source review is used during diagnosis. Evaluation uses a virtual six-axis robot model in RVIZ and does not include a physical robot.

column2: RoboFuzz: Fuzzing Robotic Systems over Robot Operating System (ROS) for Finding Correctness Bugs
column22: RoboFuzz targets ROS 2 Foxy internals and ROS 2 applications. Its primary contribution is detecting violations of physical laws, specifications, robot-domain constraints, and simulation–physical discrepancies, mapped to BSE. Separately observed type-checking, missing-validation, null-dereference, exception-handling, and unreachable-code faults are GPE. The trajectory-setpoint message-definition mismatch is ICF. The core method operates through runtime ROS graph discovery, message mutation, state monitoring, and correctness oracles, so target source code is not inherently required; source was nevertheless reviewed for oracle construction and ROS 2 was built from source for internal-layer experiments. Physical PX4 and TurtleBot3 robots were evaluated together with simulated counterparts, so Simulation Use is Hybrid.

column2: DiscoFuzzer: Discontinuity-based Vulnerability Detector for Robotic Systems
column22: DiscoFuzzer targets ROS Kinetic and dynamically mutates ROS topic-message fields. Its principal detection mechanism identifies abrupt or unexpected changes in robot outputs based on physical continuity, state consistency and behavioral relationships, corresponding to BSE. It additionally detects crashes, persistent NaN/infinity values and potential memory or mathematical implementation faults, but the paper does not provide sufficient root-cause details for every benchmark issue; therefore GPE is secondary and conservatively coded Partial. Evaluation used 20 benchmark versions from 14 ROS packages in a virtualized ROS environment, with no physical robot. The uploaded version is a non-peer-reviewed preprint.

column2: Enhancing ROS System Fuzzing through Callback Tracing
column22: R2D2 targets ROS 2 Humble and Rolling, including the ROS runtime and Navigator2, TurtleBot3, Turtlesim, and Autoware. The 39 detected bugs mainly comprise memory-management and generic synchronization defects, including OOM, overflow, UAF, double-free, null-pointer dereference, segmentation faults, memory leaks, data races, and deadlocks; therefore GPE is primary. Executor scheduling and callback-timing faults are explicitly analyzed but are not separately evaluated as a principal discovered defect family, so SEF is coded Partial. R2D2 requires source-level instrumentation of RCL/RCLCPP and sanitizer-enabled compilation. Experiments were software-only and included simulated/headless ROS applications, with no physical robot evaluation.

column2: Property-Based Testing for the Robot Operating System
column22: The approach generates property-based integration tests from HAROS-extracted ROS computation-graph models. Its primary target is orchestration and interface integration, including incorrect topic bindings, names, remappings, launch configurations, missing message flows, and unexpected changes in published or subscribed topics. User-defined behavioral and temporal contracts are separately supported and demonstrated on the Kobuki safety controller, so BSE is also covered. Crash and node-liveness detection are implemented, but no concrete programming-error instance is evaluated; therefore GPE is Partial. Source code is required because HAROS statically extracts nodes, topics, message types, and configurations from launch files and C++ source code. The preliminary experiment was executed in a virtual machine without a physical robot.

column2: Checking consistency of robot software architectures in ROS
column22: The paper targets inconsistencies in ROS node graphs and roslaunch configurations, including disconnected components, unintended connections, missing publishers, incorrect topic remappings, parameters, namespaces, and topic/service interfaces. The implemented prototype combines static launch-file analysis with sandboxed execution of ROS binaries. ROS 2 is mentioned only as future adaptation and is therefore not coded.

column2: Static-time Extraction and Analysis of the ROS Computation Graph
column22: The paper explicitly targets the original ROS version and statically reconstructs ROS computation graphs from launch files, CMake files, and C++ source code. The primary analyzed faults concern incorrect architectural relationships: mismatched publisher/subscriber types, incorrect or missing remappings, disconnected topics, problematic global names, and incomplete node communication. Queue-size queries address potential execution and message-loss problems, but no queue-induced runtime failure is directly evaluated; therefore SEF is secondary and Partial. Evaluation uses TurtleBot2 and the industrial AgRob V16 case study, with manual code and runtime inspection used only to validate extracted models.

column2: Verification of System-Wide Safety Properties of ROS Applications
column22: The HAROS safety plug-in verifies configuration-specific, system-wide behavioral properties over ROS message traces. Properties constrain message values, operating modes, command provenance and sensor-to-actuator behavior. Evaluation used the real AgRob V16 software architecture, 30 node-level specifications and four system-wide properties over two launch configurations. One unsafe counterexample was found in the map configuration. The evaluation is limited to one system and bounded model checking; the counterexample was not reproduced through runtime execution on the physical robot.

column2: A Framework for Quality Assessment of ROS Repositories
column22: HAROS is a ROS-specific, plug-in-based static-analysis framework. It evaluates source-code metrics, quality-threshold violations and coding-standard violations in ROS repositories. The evaluated corpus contains nearly 50 repositories and 180 C++ packages from 11 ROS robots. The reported indicators identify potential implementation defects and maintainability risks, but the paper does not validate whether each violation corresponds to an actual runtime failure.

column2: ROSInfer: Statically Inferring Behavioral Component Models for ROS-based Robotics Systems
column22: ROSInfer statically infers behavioral state-machine models from ROS 1 C++ source code by recognizing ROS API calls, callbacks, publishing operations, periodic loops, state variables and state transitions. Its demonstrated defect-detection use case concerns behavioral architectural composition bugs in which a component requires an input message for important functionality, but no component in the selected configuration publishes that message. Three documented Autoware.AI bugs were detected through generated PlusCal/TLA+ models and eventual-output properties. The tool and replication package, including handwritten models and evaluation data, are publicly available.

column2: Towards Automatic Inference of Behavioral Component Models for ROS-Based Robotics Systems
column22: The paper defines “behavioral architectural composition bugs” caused by incompatible behavioral assumptions among ROS components, such as waiting indefinitely for initialization messages, ignoring inputs, failing to change state, losing messages, or publishing at an unexpected frequency. ROSInfer statically infers input-output state machines from ROS C++ source code. Dynamic recovery, timing analysis and the full end-to-end evaluation are proposed future work.

column2: Lightweight Detection of Physical Unit Inconsistencies without Program Annotations
column22: The paper detects physical-unit semantic inconsistencies in ROS C++ programs, including assignment of incompatible units, comparison of quantities with different units, and addition of physically incompatible quantities. The tool analyzes ROS Indigo repositories using static analysis and a mapping from ROS message attributes to physical units. Evaluation covers 213 repositories and more than 900,000 LOC.

column2: Phriky-Units: A Lightweight, Annotation-Free Physical Unit Inconsistency Detection Tool
column22: Tool/demo paper presenting Phriky-Units, a static-analysis tool for detecting physical-unit inconsistencies in ROS C++ code. The paper summarizes an evaluation previously reported by the same authors on 213 ROS projects. It should be grouped with the full ISSTA study and should not be treated as independent empirical evidence if the SLR counts study families rather than individual publications.

column2: Phys: Probabilistic Physical Unit Assignment and Inconsistency Detection
column22: Phys uses probabilistic inference to assign physical units to variables and detect unit-semantic inconsistencies in ROS C++ software. It extends Phriky by combining ROS message-field mappings with dataflow, variable-name, computed-unit, known-symbol and conversion evidence. It is evaluated against Phriky on public ROS project files and provides a public replication artifact.

column2: PhysFrame: Type Checking Physical Frames of Reference for Robotic Systems
column22: BSE is primary because the central contribution is a frame-type system for detecting incorrect physical transformations, axis-orientation conventions, and frame-semantic inconsistencies. ICF is secondary because the tool separately detects missing frame identifiers, malformed TF-tree relationships, redundant transforms, and naming/configuration violations. The evaluation uses 180 ROS projects, including ROS Kinetic and Indigo projects. The tool and evaluation data are publicly available through Zenodo.

column2: SA4U: Practical Static Analysis for Unit Type Error Detection
column22: Non-ROS study. The actual subjects are ArduPilot and PX4 UAS firmware using MAVLink. SA4U detects physical-unit and reference-frame semantic errors through source instrumentation, simulator traces, protocol definitions and static constraint solving. ROS appears only in comparison with Phriky, Phys and PhysFrame. Recommend exclusion from the final ROS SLR corpus.

column2: UPPAAL-Based Modeling and Verification of ROS 2 Multi-threaded Execution and Operating System Reservations
column22: The primary issue is non-malicious callback blocking, starvation risk, increased latency, and OS-scheduling interference in the ROS 2 multi-threaded executor. Although the authors occasionally call these effects “vulnerabilities,” no attacker, unauthorized behavior, or missing security policy is studied; therefore, the paper is coded as reliability rather than vulnerability. The method requires callback release times, execution times, callback types, executor/thread settings, and reservation parameters, but not the target node source code. Evaluation combines executions on two real ROS 2 test systems with UPPAAL simulation/model checking. QA4 is Partial because the systems and scenarios are small-scale and the reservation-server component is checked mainly against manually constructed synthetic traces. QA5 is Partial because the complete UPPAAL model is provided, but the ROS 2 distribution, detailed machine configuration, and complete experimental implementation are not sufficiently documented for exact reproduction.

column2: A Model-Based Methodology for Automated Verification of ROS 2 Systems
column22: The proposed toolchain automates the construction of UPPAAL models for verifying ROS 2 callback latency, executor blocking, input-buffer adequacy, buffer overflow, and missed callback instances. These targets originate in ROS 2 executor scheduling and runtime execution, so SEF is the appropriate root-cause code. The paper uses “vulnerable” in the general sense of being prone to blocking, but it does not involve an attacker, unauthorized behavior, or a security-policy failure; therefore, it is coded as reliability rather than vulnerability. Source code of the analyzed ROS 2 application is not required as an analysis input: implemented systems are processed through ROS2_tracing, while conceptual systems may begin from an EMF system model. The proof of concept runs a small standalone ROS 2 system and generated UPPAAL models, without Gazebo or another robotics simulator. QA3 is Partial because several transformations and requirement-generation components remain conceptual or only partially implemented. QA4 is Partial because evaluation uses one small example, selected callback types, and no comparative baseline or comprehensive defect-detection experiment. QA5 is No because no public implementation or replication package is identified, and the transformation details are insufficient for exact independent reproduction.

column2: Formal Verification of ROS-based Robotic Applications using Timed-Automata
column22: The study directly models ROS 1 publisher–subscriber communication, queues, ros::spinOnce, callback processing, timeouts, publication rates, and message priorities. UPPAAL verification identifies queue-overflow configurations, lost sensor messages, and starvation of RandomWalker velocity commands in the Kobuki robot. Evaluation is limited to a synthetic example and one ROS robot case study, without physical execution validation or comparison with alternative approaches. Kobuki source code is public, but no dedicated replication package or UPPAAL model repository is reported.

column2: Pattern-based verification of ROS 2 applications using UPPAAL
column22: The method models ROS 2 callback releases, executor scheduling, callback execution times, priorities, communication delays, jitter, and input/output buffer utilization using reusable UPPAAL timed-automata templates. It covers both ExV1 and ExV2 single-threaded executors and evaluates ROS 2 Dashing, Eloquent, and Humble. Model traces are compared with actual ROS 2 executions in Docker. The complete UPPAAL model is made available online.

column2: Verifying ROS-Based Applications Using Timed and Stochastic Timed Automata
column22: The paper formalizes ROS 2 scheduling and communication using timed and stochastic timed automata. It verifies end-to-end reaction-time bounds under deterministic and nondeterministic execution times and probabilistic workloads. Evaluation reproduces four cases from earlier simulation-based work and studies a camera-guided industrial scenario, but it does not validate the models through actual ROS 2 or physical-robot execution. The UPPAAL models and source code are publicly available.

column2: DiNeROS: A Model-Driven Framework for Verifiable ROS Applications with Petri Nets
column22: The framework models ROS nodes, topics, services, publisher queues, dispatcher queues, callback queues, service instances, and external signals using extended Petri nets. The primary evaluated faults are queue overflows caused by insufficient or unaligned capacities. Separate behavioral faults are evaluated through contradictory or permanently false signal clauses. The approach is evaluated with a two-industrial-robot-arm sorting application, but the empirical evaluation is limited to one case study and several author-created fault scenarios. Tooling is publicly referenced, while complete replication instructions and artifact details are limited.

column2: Distributed Petri Nets for Model-Driven Verifiable Robotic Applications in ROS
column22: DiNeROS formally models ROS nodes, topics, services, channel capacities, external signals, and node-internal workflows using Petri nets. Its primary defect target is incorrect interaction and communication configuration, including topic queue overflow, unused topics, services that are never called or never return, and dead nodes. BSE is additionally assigned because the paper directly evaluates unsatisfiable signal clauses and incorrect workflow conditions. The implementation is ROS 1: it uses the ROS Master, RosJava and the common subset of Java/C++ ROS client libraries; ROS 2 support is explicitly left as future work. The verification input is a PNML-based System Model rather than target application source code. Evaluation includes two physical industrial robot arms and runtime ROS execution, not a robotics simulator. QA4 is Partial because the evaluation is based on one controlled, small-scale case study and partial state-space exploration. QA5 is Partial because a DiNeROS tooling website is provided, but no versioned replication package, complete experimental configuration, or fully documented reproduction workflow is identified in the paper.

column2: Formal Verification of ROS Based Systems Using a Linear Logic Theorem Prover
column22: The primary target is the consistency and compatibility of the ROS computational graph, including idle publishers/subscribers, publisher–subscriber type consistency, multiple publishers on one topic, component compatibility, and whether a composed node graph can satisfy a required behavior. The Kobuki bad-design case removes cmd_vel_mux, allowing two components to publish velocity commands without arbitration and causing the desired behavior property to become unprovable; this is primarily an interactioNorchitecture fault and is coded ICF. BSE is additionally assigned for the separate runtime experiment in which injected sensor faults are evaluated against explicitly defined safety rules and behavioral requirements. The study concerns ROS 1, evidenced by HAROS, ROS 1 computational graphs, Kobuki Gazebo, nodelets, and the referenced ROS Melodic application. Source dependence is Mixed: static extraction uses the application source code and launch files through HAROS, whereas the dynamic approach uses runtime node and sensor-status information. Runtime evaluation is conducted in Kobuki Gazebo rather than on a physical robot. QA4 is Partial because evaluation consists of small proof-of-concept examples without quantitative baselines, scalability analysis, or broad subjects. QA5 is Partial because experiment source code is referenced, but the linear-logic encodings are manually produced and the complete static-verification workflow is not packaged for direct reproduction.

column2: Formal Analysis and Detection for ROS2 Communication Security Vulnerability
column22: The paper formally models and experimentally tests seven ROS 2 communication attacks covering topics, services, and actions. SROS2 blocks unauthenticated attackers, but an attacker possessing intercepted security profiles can authenticate and execute all seven attacks. Unauthorized publication additionally demonstrates acceptance of forged messages from a malicious publisher. No public ROS2Tester source-code repository or full replication package is reported.

column2: ROSCallBaX: Statically Detecting Inconsistencies in Callback Function Setup of Robotic Systems
column22: ROSCallBaX statically analyzes ROS 1/ROS 2 C++ and Python source code. It models callbacks, callback groups or queues, executors or spinners, spin operations and thread associations as a composition graph, then checks nine classes of execution-setup inconsistencies. Evaluation covers 30 forum posts represented by 50 test files and 30 public ROS projects. It reports 92 inconsistencies, including 81 true positives, for an overall true-positive rate of 88.04%. A public replication artifact is provided through Zenodo.

column2: A Novel Solution for Securing Robot Communications Based on the MQTT Protocol and ROS
column22: The study proposes an MQTT-based gateway that protects remote ROS 1 communication using TLS payload encryption, X.509 certificates, client authentication, and MQTT authorization mechanisms. ROS1-LE is selected as the primary code because encrypted communication and its performance overhead are the principal implemented and experimentally evaluated security mechanism. ROS1-LNA is also Full because certificate-based client authentication is implemented in the evaluated architecture. ROS1-UTA is Partial because MQTT ACLs and restricted publish/subscribe rights are explicitly proposed, but topic-level authorization is not separately configured, attacked, or experimentally evaluated. The implementation uses ROS Kinetic on Ubuntu 16.04 and explicitly treats ROS 2 as future work. The solution operates through MQTT broker and bridge configuration without requiring the target ROS application source code. Experiments use three physical surveillance robots, not simulation. QA4 is Partial because only performance overhead is evaluated; the paper does not execute man-in-the-middle, hijacking, or unauthorized-access attacks. QA5 is Partial because the architecture, software components, platforms, durations, and metrics are reported, but the broker configuration, certificates, ACL files, LoadRunner scripts, and complete replication package are not published.

column2: From Models To Software Through Automatic Transformations: An AADL To ROS End-to-End Toolchain
column22: The toolchain transforms an AADL architecture into ROS 1 C++ packages while preserving nodes, typed ports, connections, topic names, publishers, subscribers, services, timers and launch relationships. Its main reliability relevance is preventing architectural and interface inconsistencies between the model and generated ROS implementation. Build artifacts are also generated, but no concrete build-fault experiment is presented. The autonomous-wheelchair application is only briefly described, without a systematic defect evaluation or public replication package.

column2: On the (In)Security of Secure ROS2
column22: The paper systematically analyzes the ROS 2/SROS2 implementation and identifies four security vulnerabilities across ROS 2 Eloquent, Foxy, and Galactic. ROS2-ICAPP is the primary code because V1 and V2 arise from inadequate protection and synchronization of permission policies: an adversarial robot can reuse an expired but validly signed permission file or refuse node/participant reinitialization, thereby retaining revoked publish/subscribe privileges. ROS2-ILE covers V3 and V4: insecure default signing without encryption exposes DDS participant and topology metadata, while plaintext and over-inclusive permission files leak security-policy information. The analysis requires the ROS 2 RCL/RMW source code to construct code-property graphs and abstract communication-related functions. Evaluation combines Gazebo experiments with three OpenRMF workloads and a physical testbed using three TurtleBot 3 Waffle Pi robots and AWS cloud infrastructure. The authors also evaluate a private-broadcast-encryption defense through formal analysis, attack mitigation, latency benchmarks, and CPU/RAM measurements. Supporting models, implementation details, exploits, and the open-source defense are reported as publicly available.

column2: ROSDiscover: Statically Detecting Run-Time Architecture Misconfigurations in Robotics Systems
column22: ROSDiscover reconstructs component ports, parameters and connectors from C++ source code, CMake files and ROS launch files, then checks the recovered architecture using first-order logic rules. It detects topic-name and message-type mismatches, incorrect topic remapping, dangling publishers/subscribers and architecture-related parameter misconfigurations. Evaluation uses five real ROS systems and a dataset of 29 historical bugs; 19 bugs fall within the implemented scope and 8 are detected directly. The implementation, dataset, Docker images, scripts and results are publicly available.
